interest: This file provides a fascinating case study in Allied economic intelligence during World War II, illustrating how the Axis capture of Southeast Asian natural rubber was critically undermined by a single bottleneck: high-grade carbon black necessary for tyre compounding. It documents the close liaison and intelligence-sharing apparatus between the British Ministry of Economic Warfare (MEW) and American agencies such as the Board of Economic Warfare, the Coordinator of Information (COI), and the War Production Board. Furthermore, it contains rare and highly specific industrial data on petrochemical and chemical facilities across the Japanese empire, including natural gas extraction in colonial Taiwan (Kinsui, Chikuto, Bochirin) and carbide-acetylene plants in colonial Korea (Chosen Chisso at Konan), as well as insights into Japan's attempts to acquire German industrial processes (such as the Degussa process) through barter.
overview: This file (894.6176 Agriculture., Trees., Japan, Rubber., File 1350) consists of Despatch No. 4008 dated June 2, 1942, from James Somerville, Liaison Officer with the Ministry of Economic Warfare at the U.S. Embassy in London, transmitting to the Secretary of State a secret British intelligence report prepared by the MEW's Enemy Resources Department on May 12, 1942, titled 'Carbon Black Supply Position in the Japanese Rubber Industry.' The report assesses that despite Japan's acquisition of abundant raw rubber supplies in Southeast Asia, her military and civilian motor vehicle and aircraft tyre manufacture faced a critical vulnerability due to an acute shortage of tyre-grade carbon black, which prior to the war was produced exclusively in the United States and Germany. With U.S. exports cut off in early 1941 and German exportable surpluses doubtful, the intelligence survey analyzes Japanese domestic production in Formosa and Japan proper, evaluates pre-war import trends and strategic stockpiles (estimated at nil to eight months' supply entering 1942), and examines Japan's potential expedients, including diluting stocks, bartering rubber for German black, using inferior substitutes like zinc oxide and china clay, and developing domestic synthesis methods.

subfiles.about: Transmittal of a British Ministry of Economic Warfare intelligence report analyzing Japan's supply position and acute deficit of tyre-grade carbon black.
subfiles.from: James Somerville, Liaison Officer with the Ministry of Economic Warfare, American Embassy, London
subfiles.summary: James Somerville, Liaison Officer at the U.S. Embassy in London, forwards five copies of a secret British Ministry of Economic Warfare intelligence survey dated May 12, 1942, to the Secretary of State. The despatch summarizes the core finding that while Japan possessed abundant raw rubber, her motor tyre production was acutely vulnerable due to the lack of high-quality carbon black, produced exclusively in the United States and Germany. Somerville notes that because Germany was unlikely to have an exportable surplus, Japan was restricted to using inferior substitutes (which halved tyre lifespan) or aggressively improving low-grade domestic output. The despatch also records wide dissemination of the report to U.S. agencies including the Board of Economic Warfare, Coordinator of Information, and War Production Board.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4008 from London Embassy transmitting MEW report on carbon black in the Japanese rubber industry
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.

subfiles.about: Detailed British intelligence assessment of Japan's carbon black requirements, domestic production, import trends, and strategic stockpile position for tyre manufacturing.
subfiles.from: Enemy Resources Department, Ministry of Economic Warfare
subfiles.summary: This secret Ministry of Economic Warfare survey comprehensively assesses the critical role of carbon black in Japan's rubber manufacturing, emphasizing that motor and aircraft tyres accounted for 75-80% of total demand (about 4,000 tons per year). Prior to the Pacific War, Japan relied almost entirely on U.S. imports for tyre-grade black, which peaked in 1940 at nearly 8,000 tons before being halted by American export licence controls and asset freezes in 1941. The report details domestic capacity in Formosa (derived from natural gas) and Japan proper (acetylene and coal tar distillates), profiling producers such as Taiwan Kogyo Kaisha, Nippon Sekiyu Kaisha, and Chosen Chisso Kaisha, while concluding their product remained deficient in quality for tyres. Statistical appendices analyze domestic output, pre-war imports, and estimated stocks entering 1942 (calculated at zero to eight months' supply, or up to 21 months under dilution), outlining Japan's strategic dilemmas between German barter, dilution, and inferior fillers like zinc oxide and china clay.
subfiles.title: Ministry of Economic Warfare Report: Carbon Black Supply Position in the Japanese Rubber Industry
subfiles.to: British and Allied government departments and American Embassy
